THOUGHT: This 34-year-old male with advanced AIDS (CD4 count 36/mm³) presents with acute, painless, unilateral visual loss and floaters (black spots) in the right eye. The fundoscopic findings—granular yellow-white perivascular opacities ("cotton-wool spots" are not described; rather, the description suggests retinal infiltrates or necrosis) and multiple dot-blot hemorrhages—are highly characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. CMV retinitis is the most common opportunistic ocular infection in patients with AIDS and CD4 counts <50/mm³. The absence of pain, unilateral involvement, and rapid onset over 2 days align with CMV retinitis. Other considerations include:
- Toxoplasma chorioretinitis: Typically presents with focal necrotic retinitis and vitritis, often with anterior uveitis (pain, redness, photophobia)—not seen here; also less common than CMV at this CD4 level.
- Syphilitic uveitis/retinitis: Can cause similar findings but usually associated with systemic symptoms or other stigmata (e.g., rash, neurologic signs); no history provided, and fundus findings are less typical (more vasculitic, with sheathing, not granular opacities + hemorrhages).
- Pneumocystis or fungal chorioretinitis: Extremely rare; no systemic respiratory symptoms or fungemia markers.
- HIV retinopathy: Causes cotton-wool spots and hemorrhages but is asymptomatic (no vision loss) and does not cause granular yellow-white opacities or necrotizing retinitis.
- Kaposi’s sarcoma of the retina: Very rare; would present as violaceous, raised, vascular lesions—not granular opacities or hemorrhages.
The history of prior AIDS-defining illnesses (Kaposi’s sarcoma, fungal esophagitis) confirms profound immunosuppression and supports the likelihood of CMV reactivation. CMV retinitis classically begins as a peripheral, granular, yellow-white retinal infiltrate with hemorrhages, progressing centrally if untreated—exactly matching the fundus description.

DIAGNOSIS: Cytomegalovirus retinitis
